### Company description

Vornado Realty L.P. is the operating partnership through which Vornado Realty Trust holds substantially all of its assets; the trust is sole general partner and owned about 91.2% of the common limited partnership interest at 2026-09-30. Creditor figures here use the partnership's own statements; the trust's per-share and funds-from-operations measures are context only. The business is a Manhattan-weighted office landlord with street retail, residential, THE MART in Chicago and a controlling interest in an office complex in San Francisco; the New York metropolitan area supplies 88% of NOI at share and office about 78% in FY2025. The Park Avenue development venture named in the findings is the venture on 350 Park Avenue formed on 2026-10-20, which is separate from the 49.0% interest in the Park Avenue Plaza office building bought in June 2026.

Rental revenues were 87.39% of nine-month revenues, from leases whose third-quarter New York office signings ran 9.5 years on average, so the revenue model is contractual rent with escalations and tenant reimbursements, plus smaller fee income from cleaning, management and leasing. That gives good cash-flow visibility and supports debt service, but the concentration in one market and one property type means a Manhattan office downturn would hit nearly all cash flow at once, and the partnership's ability to refinance depends on lenders' views of that market.
Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_vno-20260930.htm.jsonl, pages 3, 18, 50, 57, 67; 10-K_2025-12-31_vno-20251231.htm.jsonl, pages 8, 16; Business & governance (CP-1A); calculation CALC-27
### Ownership and group structure

The trust is the sole general partner with exclusive control of day-to-day management, third-party Class A unitholders hold about 8.8% of common units with a right to tender for cash, and the trust has 48.79 million preferred shares outstanding whose distributions the partnership funds. Chairman and chief executive Steven Roth also leads Alexander's, and Interstate Properties and its partners held about 7.1% of the trust's shares and 26.0% of Alexander's at 2025-12-31, which the annual report calls substantial influence. For creditors the structure means the partnership's unsecured claims rank alongside other partnership-level liabilities but behind the creditors of operating subsidiaries and consolidated joint ventures, and cash leaves the partnership first to preferred distributions and then to the trust's common dividend; guarantors, a restricted group and the legal rank of each instrument are not established because the governing documents are not supplied.
Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_vno-20260930.htm.jsonl, pages 3, 6, 12, 29; 10-K_2025-12-31_vno-20251231.htm.jsonl, pages 33, 38; Business & governance (CP-1A)
### Revenue drivers and pricing power

Revenue is predictable and largely recurring but cyclical in its re-leasing. Leases are long (9.5 years on third-quarter New York office signings), expirations are spread (6.1%, 6.2% and 6.3% of New York office square feet in 2026, 2027 and 2028), and weighted average escalated office rent rose from USD 80.01 per square foot in 2021 to USD 90.56 in 2025 while occupancy moved between 88.8% and 92.2%. Pricing power is real in prime office, where second-generation rents rose 23.5% on a GAAP basis over nine months, and absent in retail, where cash rents fell 7.1%. The mechanism is that rolling 2026 expiring office rents of USD 79.82 per square foot to the USD 85 to 95 management expects on re-leasing raises NOI, while tenants' hybrid-work and space-reduction choices set the vacancy risk, so the credit implication is steady organic growth that must still outrun a higher interest bill.
### Cost structure and margin resilience

Operating costs are largely fixed in the short run: mortgage payments, real estate taxes and maintenance do not fall when rents fall, the building-services workforce is unionised, and nine-month consolidated operating expenses rose 4.37% against revenue growth of 2.38%, taking the consolidated NOI margin to 48.47% from 49.45%. Same-store operations did better, with NOI at share up 8.4%, so the margin pressure came from acquisitions, development and non-reimbursable costs rather than the stabilised portfolio. Margins can be defended against modest volume pressure through reimbursements and escalations but not against a deep occupancy fall or a sharp rise in wage and energy costs, so operating leverage cuts both ways for interest cover. Multiemployer pension contributions of USD 9.65 million and health plan contributions of USD 34.88 million in FY2025 sit inside operating expenses, and withdrawal liability is not quantified.
Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_vno-20260930.htm.jsonl, pages 52, 65, 67; 10-K_2025-12-31_vno-20251231.htm.jsonl, pages 14, 19, 150; calculation CALC-26
### Capital intensity and cash conversion

Capital intensity is high and part of it is discretionary. Leasing capital absorbs 13.1% of initial rent on New York office space signed in nine months, additions to real estate and development spending were USD 273.91 million in nine months, and non-cash rent adjustments of USD 116.34 million mean cash NOI at share was 86.72% of NOI at share. Growth capital can be deferred, but the remaining USD 195.73 million on the Fifth Avenue office redevelopment and the cash call from mid-2028 on the Park Avenue venture are commitments in practice. EBITDA therefore converts weakly into free cash flow: after cash interest, capital spending and preferred distributions the twelve-month figure is a shortfall of USD 10.74 million, so deleveraging has to come from asset sales or EBITDA growth.
Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_vno-20260930.htm.jsonl, pages 58, 65–67, 70–73; Financial foundation (CP-1); calculation CALC-13; calculation CALC-14; calculation CALC-25
### Porter's five forces

Competitive rivalry is the force that matters: the partnership competes with many owners and developers, some willing to accept lower returns, on rents, concessions, location and building quality, and tenants have moved to modern amenitised buildings; the mechanism is higher concessions and capital to hold Class A status, and the implication is that leasing capital stays near 12% to 13% of initial rent. New entrants take the form of newer, more amenitised competing buildings in the same market, which the annual report names as a risk to leasing and effective rents, and the threat of substitutes is real through hybrid work, co-working, sublease space and artificial-intelligence-driven space reduction, which could cut demand for office space in the largest tenant industries, financial services at 23% and technology at 13% of rents. Buyer power is moderate: no tenant exceeds 10% of revenues and the ten largest are 26.9% of rent, but large tenants negotiate free rent and allowances. Supplier power is moderate: building-services labour is unionised and construction and renovation costs are named as a factor in results, and the annual report says it is not assured that increases in operating costs can be passed through to tenants in full.
### PEST

PEST factors matter through three channels only. Economic: base rates and refinancing conditions set interest cost on the USD 1,972.54 million of floating-rate consolidated debt, and New York employment and tourism set rents. Political and regulatory: New York City's Local Law 97 carbon limits, the State's grid decarbonisation mandate and the gas-ban bill could raise operating and retrofit costs and decrease cash available for obligations, though the annual report states no material effect to date. Social and technological: hybrid work and artificial-intelligence-driven space use set long-run demand for office space. Other political and social factors do not appear to be a primary credit driver on the provided materials.
### SWOT

Strengths in credit terms: leasing momentum and rising occupancy in New York office; ten largest tenants at 26.9% of rent with no tenant above 10% of revenues; unsecured maturities beyond April 2029; liquidity of USD 1,768.78 million; asset values above book. Weaknesses: leverage of 8.08x trailing EBITDA and 8.88x look-through NOI at share; free cash flow near zero; secured maturities of USD 2,780.00 million in 2027 and 2028; concentration in one market and property type. Opportunities that could improve credit quality: sales or joint-venture monetisations at values above book that repay debt, and delivery of the Fifth Avenue office redevelopment in 2027. Threats that could weaken it: a sharp rise in vacancy, refinancing at higher coupons as hedges expire in 2027, joint-venture equity calls and recourse support for the Park Avenue venture's construction loan, and a lower share price tightening a market-based covenant.

### Financial profile and credit quality

The financial profile is weaker than the business profile. Consolidated debt of USD 7,448.31 million is 0.48x total assets at book, but EBITDA derived by Financial foundation covers cash interest only 2.89x and trailing leverage excluding gains of 8.47x is above the FY2025 underlying 7.74x. Trend is mixed: underlying leverage improved in 2025 and has risen again in 2026 as borrowings funded joint-venture investments, acquisitions and repurchases, while look-through leverage on NOI at share rose from 8.72x to 8.88x. Main supports are liquidity, distant unsecured maturities and asset values; main constraints are leverage, near-zero free cash flow and the secured wall; key missing datapoints are covenant levels, ratings, the minority share of consolidated joint-venture debt and a ladder at 2026-09-30.

The debt stack at 2026-09-30 is USD 4,869.54 million of mortgages (USD 3,340.00 million fixed at a weighted 4.98% and USD 1,529.54 million floating at 5.65%), USD 850.00 million of senior unsecured notes (USD 350.00 million due 2031 and USD 500.00 million due 2033), an USD 850.00 million term loan to February 2031 and USD 918.00 million drawn on two revolvers with USD 2,130.00 million of commitments; carrying value is USD 39.23 million below principal after financing costs. ### Outlook, tailwinds and headwinds

Over 12 to 24 months the tailwinds are lease-up and rent growth in New York office (the Fifth Avenue office redevelopment is due for delivery in 2027), a lower development outlay once it completes, and a consolidated debt stack with no unsecured maturity before April 2029; the headwinds are the end of the Seventh Avenue waiver of default interest in March 2027, USD 480.00 million of mortgages due in 2027 and USD 2,300.00 million in 2028, expiry of swaps and caps between February 2027 and October 2027, and a distribution of about USD 153.30 million in the fourth quarter if the 2025 rate is repeated. Over 3 to 5 years the equity call of about USD 290.00 million from mid-2028 on a USD 6,250.00 million development, drawing of its USD 3,300.00 million construction loan (about USD 1,191.30 million at the partnership's 36.1% effective share if fully drawn, an analyst inference), and the preferred equity return on the Fifth Avenue and Times Square joint venture moving from 4.75% to a formula after April 2029 are the main swing factors. The sector tailwind is tenants' preference for high-quality, modern, well-located buildings, which favours the partnership's Class A office; sector headwinds are hybrid work, tenant space reduction and retail weakness.

### Downside scenario

The initiating condition is a Manhattan office leasing slowdown, with tenants cutting space under hybrid work and artificial-intelligence-driven reductions while base rates stay high. The first operating break is lower occupancy: a return of New York office occupancy to the 88.8% of 2024-12-31, 4.2 percentage points below 93.0%, would vacate about 716,142 square feet of the partnership's share at USD 90.56 of annual escalated rent, or USD 64.85 million of rent, 7.38% of trailing EBITDA excluding gains, assuming no expense savings and no re-letting. The financial transmission is EBITDA of USD 814.19 million, total debt over EBITDA of 9.15x and, with a one percentage point rise in base rates costing USD 11.48 million, cash interest of USD 330.28 million and cover of 2.47x. The liquidity and refinancing consequence is that USD 2,780.00 million of mortgages and the USD 244.54 million Seventh Avenue loan must be refinanced into weaker property income, while the equity call begins in mid-2028; USD 1,188.28 million of undrawn revolver capacity, no unsecured maturity before April 2029, USD 286.59 million of repurchase authority the board need not use, deferral of the remaining Fifth Avenue office spend, asset sales and the non-recourse nature of property loans other than guarantees of about USD 193.36 million are the levers. Resilience looks sufficient to avoid a liquidity event over 24 months, but the equity cushion would thin, and the observable triggers are occupancy below 91.2%, negative second-generation rent spreads, revolver drawings above USD 918.00 million and no refinancing progress six months before a maturity.
Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_vno-20260930.htm.jsonl, pages 27, 42, 57–58, 70, 73, 77, 79; 10-K_2025-12-31_vno-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 52; calculation CALC-20; calculation CALC-24

The ranked drivers are in the materiality register in the appendix: six negatives led by look-through leverage and the 2027 to 2028 mortgage wall, and three positives, liquidity with distant unsecured maturities, New York office leasing momentum and asset values above book. The two that decide the view are whether EBITDA grows faster than debt and whether the secured wall is refinanced without paydown.

### Issuer matrix

Revenue durability is strong because leases are long and tenants diversified, with the downside path through office vacancy and rent resets. Margin resilience is average, with the path through operating costs that do not fall with rents. Free cash flow conversion is weak, with the path through capital spending and distributions exceeding operating cash flow. Liquidity buffer is strong over twelve months, with the path through a mortgage-market shock that forces revolver use. Refinancing capacity is average, resting on one unsecured issue in January 2026 and the secured wall, with the path through higher coupons. Governance and financial policy is average, with the path through buybacks and joint-venture equity while leverage is high. Primary downside path: weaker office income meeting the 2027 and 2028 mortgage maturities and the mid-2028 equity call with cash flow that is already near zero after capital spending and distributions.
Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_vno-20260930.htm.jsonl, pages 57–58, 70, 73; calculation CALC-13; calculation CALC-15; calculation CALC-17

### Overall credit view

Overall, Vornado Realty L.P. presents a strong business profile supported by a leasing-led Manhattan office franchise at 93.0% occupancy, a tenant base with none above 10% of revenues and liquidity of USD 1,768.78 million, but credit quality is constrained by leverage of 8.08x trailing EBITDA and 8.88x look-through NOI at share and by free cash flow that is near zero after capital spending and preferred distributions. Cash-flow durability appears adequate because rents are contractual and rising, but not strong because cash conversion lags and discretionary spending runs ahead of deleveraging. Refinancing capacity is likely to depend on lenders' appetite for Manhattan office mortgages in 2027 and 2028, on hedge costs, and on the partnership's willingness to pause repurchases and sell assets. The primary downside path is weaker office income meeting the secured maturity wall and the mid-2028 equity call. Further analysis would require covenant levels and agreements, agency ratings and market pricing, the minority share of consolidated joint-venture debt, the Park Avenue venture's agreement and a ladder at 2026-09-30. Fundamental credit completed. Top risk: a 2027 to 2028 refinancing squeeze on already high leverage.

## Gaps

- The maturity ladder at 2026-09-30 is not printed. The ladder used here updates the ladder at 2025-12-31 for the documented 2026 refinancings and reconciles to mortgage principal of USD 4,869.54 million, but an unreported prepayment or extension would change the 2027 and 2028 amounts; this is a medium-severity gap that a ladder at 2026-09-30 would close.

- Covenant levels are not printed anywhere, compliance with the financial covenants is stated only as at 2025-12-31, and the definition of market capitalization is not given, so covenant headroom is not calculable; the annual report names total debt to total assets, secured debt to total assets, EBITDA to interest expense, fixed charges and unencumbered assets to unsecured debt as covenant families, and the agreements' own EBITDA and interest definitions differ from the derived EBITDA over cash interest paid used here; this is a medium-severity gap that the credit agreements and indentures would close.

- No agency rating, outlook, bond price or spread is supplied, so market access is judged from one unsecured issue in January 2026 only; this is a medium-severity gap that rating reports and dated quotes would close.

- The total minority share of consolidated joint-venture debt is not stated, so look-through debt attributable to the partnership cannot be computed and the figures of 8.88x and 10.28x overstate it by an unknown amount, of which USD 360.00 million is the minority share of the San Francisco mortgage; this is a medium-severity gap that a schedule of consolidated joint-venture debt by owner would close.

- The market-risk table totals the pro rata share of non-consolidated debt but gives no maturities, so the refinancing profile of USD 2,732.55 million of joint-venture debt is not established; this is a medium-severity gap that a joint-venture debt schedule would close.

- The construction loan of the Park Avenue development venture, USD 3,300.00 million, has no stated guarantee or recourse terms and is not yet part of pro rata debt; if fully drawn it would add about USD 1,191.30 million at the partnership's effective share, an analyst inference; this is a medium-severity gap that the venture agreement would close.

- No peer set is supplied, so the judgement that leverage near eight times is high rests on the partnership's own history and general credit norms rather than a comparison with other office landlords; this is a low-severity gap.

- Management gives no guidance and no forecast is supplied, so the outlook and downside illustration are analyst judgement; the downside illustration assumes no expense savings and no re-letting; this is a low-severity gap.
- Pro forma net debt after the 2026-10-20 joint venture closing is not established because the filing gives no cash effect; this is a low-severity gap that the next quarterly report would close.

- The outcome of the PENN 1 ground rent arbitration and litigation is uncertain, with annual rent of USD 15.00 million being paid against a possible USD 20.22 million retroactive to June 2023; this is a low-severity gap.
- No filing or release after the third-quarter report signed on 2026-11-02 is supplied, so events in the sixteen days to the as-of date are not covered; this is a low-severity gap.
